etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bodily; equivalent to body +‎ -ly.

definitions.definition: Of, relating to, or concerning the body.
Having a body or material form; physical; corporeal.

quote.citation: 1709 May 25 (Gregorian calendar), Isaac Bickerstaff [et al., pseudonyms; Richard Steele et al.], “Saturday, May 14, 1709”, in The Tatler, number 15; republished in [Richard Steele], editor, The Tatler, […], London stereotype edition, volume I, London: I. Walker and Co.;  […], 1822, →OCLC:
quote.text: You are a mere spirit, and have no knowledge of the bodily part of us.The spelling has been modernized.

quote.citation: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:

quote.text: For in him dwelleth all the fulneſſe of the Godhead bodily.

quote.citation: 1883, Robert Louis Stevenson, “The Voyage”, in Treasure Island‎Wikisource:
quote.text: In I got bodily into the apple barrel, and found there was scarce an apple left; but sitting down there in the dark, what with the sound of the waters and the rocking movement of the ship, I had either fallen asleep or was on the point of doing so when a heavy man sat down with rather a clash close by.

definitions.definition: Pertaining to the whole body or mass; wholly.

quote.text: The papering of one side of the room had dropped down bodily, with fragments of plaster adhering to it, and almost blocked up the door.

quote.citation: 1958, Jacob Viner, The Long View and the Short, page 112:
quote.text: It is true that in adopting the short view many of the younger economists have not merely taken over the lay notions bodily.
